previous_admission_summary.summary_paragraph: Mr. Johnson, a male with a history of kidney transplant, type 2 diabetes, hypertension, and hyperlipidemia, was admitted for symptomatic in-stent restenosis of the renal artery to his transplanted kidney. He presented with elevated blood pressure, and prior ultrasound showed increased renal artery velocities. He underwent elective balloon angioplasty of the stenotic segment without complications. He remained hemodynamically stable throughout, with no change in kidney function. His pain was controlled, and he tolerated diet advancement. He was discharged home on day two with continued immunosuppressive, antihypertensive, and dual antiplatelet therapy, and instructions to follow up with vascular surgery in two weeks.

Discharge Instructions:
Dear Mr. ___,

It was a pleasure caring for you on your recent hospitalization 
at ___. You came to the hospital because you were having 
difficulty urinating. We found that you had a urinary tract 
infection. We treated you with antibiotics and your symptoms 
improved. You will need to continue antibiotics to complete a 
total 14-day course (last day on ___. You also had acute 
kidney injury, but your creatinine (a measure of your kidney 
function) improved back to baseline by the time of discharge. We 
stopped your lisinopril because this can worsen kidney function 
-- you should restart it after talking to your PCP.

You were found to have an infection in your colon (known as 
Clostridium difficile, or C. diff) and will need to take 
vancomycin for 4 weeks; please take it four times a day (last 
day on ___.

Your tacrolimus level was found to be low, so your dose of 
tacrolimus was increased to 2.5mg daily.

You were started on a medication called doxazosin (Cardura) to 
help with your urinary flow and to try and prevent you from 
retaining urine. This medication can also lower your blood 
pressure, so we decreased your dose of carvedilol.

Please take your water pill (furosemide) twice as day as you 
have been doing at home. Weigh yourself daily and call your 
primary care physician if your weight increased by more than 3 
pounds.
